7.24.m: Sūta said: Having heard the fruit of Ekādaśī, Jaimini, well pleased, then / spoke this with folded hands to Lord Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana:
Jaimini said: The glorification of Lord Viṣṇu has been heard by me through your grace; / tell the glorification of Tulasī, which destroys the sins of those who hear.
Vyāsa said: This divine Tulasī is always to be served by all the gods headed by Indra, O Brahmin; / she bestows the fruits of the four aims of life.
In heaven, on earth, and in the underworld, Tulasī is hard to attain for the virtuous; / devotion unto her truly brings the attainment of the fruits of the four aims of life.
Even where a single Tulasī plant stands, O best [of sages], / right there are all the thirty gods, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others.
Keśava resides in the middle of her leaf, and Prajāpati at the tip of the leaf; / Śiva always resides in the stalk of the leaf of Tulasī.
Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Gāyatrī, and Caṇḍikā, / and all the other wives of the gods live in her leaves.
Indra, Agni, Yama, Nairṛta, Varuṇa, / Pavana, and Kubera dwell in her branches.
All the planets beginning with the sun, the Viśvedevas, always the / Vasus, the munis, and all the celestial ṛṣis,
and whatever sacred bathing places exist upon the earth in the midst of crores of universes, / they all indeed dwell resorting to the Tulasī leaf.
He who serves Tulasī endowed with a devotional disposition / has served the sacred places and the gods headed by Brahmā.
Those who cut away the thickets of weeds growing at the root of Tulasī— / Hari destroys from that very moment the sin of slaying a Brahmin that resides in their bodies.
In the hot season, O best of the twice-born, having watered Tulasī / with fragrant, cool waters, a man will attain liberation.
And he who provides an awning or an umbrella for her, / especially during the hot seasons, is freed from all sins.
The person who sprinkles Tulasī in the month of Vaiśākha with continuous streams of water / constantly obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
Even he who waters Tulasī with only a handful of water / reaches heaven, free from all sin.
If ever an excellent man should sprinkle Tulasī with milk, / Lakṣmī becomes permanent in his home, O Brahmin-seer.
He who plasters the base of Tulasī with cow dung / and sweeps it clean, O Brahmin-seer, hear the meritorious fruit of that:
as many particles of dust as are removed from there, O Jaimini, / for that many thousands of kalpas he rejoices with Viṣṇu.
He who places a lamp at the foot of Tulasī at twilight / goes to the abode of Viṣṇu together with a crore of [ancestors of his] family.
He who protects Tulasī from cows, dogs, donkeys, humans, / and children—Keśava always protects him.
The man who plants Tulasī with devotion, / having died, attains the supreme liberation; of this there is no doubt.
The excellent man who looks upon Tulasī with devotion in the morning / obtains the imperishable fruit of the very vision of Viṣṇu.
The man who bows to Tulasī endowed with devotion, / his life span, strength, fame, wealth, and lineage increase.
By the mere remembrance of Tulasī all sin is destroyed; / by the mere touching of Tulasī the diseases of men are eradicated.
He who eats an auspicious Tulasī leaf which removes all sins, / the sin residing within his body is destroyed from that moment.
The man who wears a garland made of Tulasī wood / has no sin in his body; this is the truth spoken by me.
He who bears upon his head the water that has dripped from a Tulasī leaf / obtains the merit arising from bathing in the Gaṅgā; there is no doubt in this.
Having worshipped auspicious Tulasī with devotion using dūrvā grass, unbroken rice grains, flowers, and food offerings, / a man obtains the fruit of worshipping Viṣṇu.

By whom divine Tulasī has ever been worshipped with food offerings, flowers, fine incense, and ghee lamps— / which bestows dharma, wealth, pleasure, and the supreme nectar—what need has he, O Brahmins, of the practices of venerating the feet of Viṣṇu?

Those who plant in faultless places Tulasī, who is served by the host of gods and brings satisfaction to Hari— / Hari, Murāri, the lord of the three worlds, being pleased, swiftly gives them the supreme state, O Brahmin.

Sacrifice, vows, worship of the ancestors, worship of Acyuta, gift-giving, and whatever other auspicious deed men / perform in a faultless place at the foot of Tulasī, all of those indeed become imperishable.

Whatever religious act a man performs on earth without tulasī, which is dearest to Nārāyaṇa, / all that becomes utterly fruitless, O best of the twice-born; even the lotus-eyed god of gods is not pleased.

A man who looks upon auspicious, pure tulasī with a devotional disposition during journeys, indeed, / attains all the fruit of his journey swiftly through the grace of Hari; this is my most firm statement.

Setting aside fragrant flowers—the mandāra, kunda, lotus, and others—the infinite, sole lord of the worlds / joyfully accepts tulasī, which is full of good qualities, even when dried, as a protection that destroys abundant sins.

Uprooting tulasī, which is the source resembling a vine of nectar, and casting it onto the ground out of ignorance, / those sinners—Narahari, who loves tulasī, truly takes away their prosperity forever.
Those men who continually pass urine, feces, and filth at the base of tulasī, / a shelter for deities—Hari quickly seizes the wealth of those who have accumulated sins.
"For the worship of Nārāyaṇa I pluck you; homage be to you! / Keśava is not satisfied even with flowers such as pārijāta and fragrances
without you; therefore I pluck you, O auspicious one. / Without you, O highly fortunate one, all ritual action is fruitless.
Therefore, O goddess tulasī, I pluck [you]; be a granter of boons! / Whatever pain arising from plucking may occur in your heart, O goddess,
forgive that, O mistress of the universe! O tulasī, I bow to you." / Having recited these mantras with folded hands, the Vaiṣṇava person,
clapping both hands twice, plucks the tulasī leaf / in such a way that no branch of the tulasī tree is shaken, O best of the twice-born.
When a branch is broken in plucking a leaf, O goddess, / then pain arises in the heart of Viṣṇu, the lord of tulasī.
Even with an old leaf that has fallen onto the ground from the tip of a branch, / Govinda, the crusher of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, should be worshipped.
He who worships the lord Acyuta with tender tulasī leaves / swiftly attains everything, whatever he desires in his heart.
Jaimini said: / Which tree is equal to the tulasī tree, O bull among the twice-born? / That I wish to know; speak, O son of Satyavatī!
Vyāsa said: / Just as tulasī is always dearest to Viṣṇu, O twice-born, / so the dhātrī, which destroys all sins, is dearest to him.
Whatever deities dwell resorting to the tulasī tree, / they all dwell at the foot of the āmalakī, O best of the twice-born.
The sacred waters such as the Gaṅgā are also right there, O best of the twice-born, / wherever the pure dhātrī, Viṣṇu's dearest, stands.
Whatever action—inauspicious or auspicious—is performed / by men at the foot of an āmalakī, O twice-born, that truly becomes inexhaustible.
He who worships Hari with pure, fresh leaves of the dhātrī / is released from the snare of sins and attains union with Hari.
Wherever the dhātrī and goddess tulasī do not stand, O Jaimini, / that place becomes impure, and one cannot obtain the fruit of one's rites.
In whose hermitage the auspicious dhātrī and tulasī do not stand, / all ritual action performed by him surely comes to nothing.
In whose dwelling there is neither dhātrī nor tulasī, O earth-god, / by him misfortune, all sins, and Kali have been pleased.
In that place, O best of the twice-born, where there is neither dhātrī nor tulasī, / that place is to be known as equal to a cremation ground by those who see reality.
Wherever the dhātrī and tulasī stand, all the gods are there; / where there is not a leaf of dhātrī or tulasī, all sins are right there.
A wise man who wears a garland of dhātrī fruits that removes sins— / Viṣṇu constantly abides with Śrī, resorting to his body.
The wise person who wears a necklace of dhātrī wood— / all the deities abide, resorting to his body.
Whatever action a man performs while wearing a garland of dhātrī fruits, / all of that, whether auspicious or inauspicious, is declared inexhaustible.
The man who knows all reality and eats a dhātrī fruit— / all sin residing within his body is destroyed.
He who wears a garland made of dhātrī fruits, O best of the twice-born— / listen as I speak of its supreme glorification, which removes all sins.
Even if his death should occur in a cremation ground due to fate, / he obtains the merit born of dying in the Gaṅgā; there is no doubt.
Seeing him, all sinners are instantly released / from terrible snares of sin accumulated over hundreds of millions of births.
O best of the twice-born, he who daily takes paste of dhātrī fruits / gains merit day by day; he attains it without doubt.
He who destroys a dhātrī tree, which is the shelter of all the hosts of gods, / deals a blow to Hari's body; there is no doubt in this.
The dhātrī consists of all the gods, and is especially dear to Keśava; / even by Brahmā its excellence cannot be adequately expressed.
The man who knows all truths and offers devotion to dhātrī and tulasī, / having enjoyed all pleasures, at the end attains liberation through the grace of Hari.

7.25.m: Jaimini said: / Once again, O highly fortunate one, tell in detail of the sin-destroying [power] of tulasī / and the glorification of honoring guests.
Sūta said: / Then the greatly splendid Vyāsa began to speak, O best of the twice-born, / of the glorification of tulasī, which destroys the sins of those who hear it.
Vyāsa said: / This tulasī is Mahālakṣmī herself, beloved of the Lord of existence; / therefore, O Jaimini, people do not look upon her with the notion of a tree.
Just as a mortal continually serves tulasī on earth, / even so the gods together with Indra serve him in the abode of the deities.
Wherever this tulasī, whose nature is the supreme brahman, stands, / right there is all well-being; this is firmly declared by me.
A person, even though sinful, who at the time of death receives water / that has dripped from a tulasī leaf, goes to the presence of Hari.
Whoever bears the mark of tulasī-clay at the time of death, / freed from all sins, goes to the city of the wielder of the discus.
One who has a tulasī leaf on his mouth, head, or ears / at the time of death, O best of the twice-born, the son of the Sun is not his master.
There was a wise man named Pavitra, who knew the supreme truth; / he had a brāhmaṇa wife named Bahulā,
Born of a good family, virtuous, devoted to the service of her husband, / childless—there is a certain best of the twice-born named Pati.
this Pavitra made friends with him, who was devoted to serving twice-borns. / Then, through eagerness for conversation with Anapatyapati, that excellent man,
this Pavitra, sat out of affection upon a single excellent seat. / Meanwhile, a good twice-born of great splendor named Lomaśa,
coming along, saw the two of them narrating wonderful stories. / Then, seeing that brāhmaṇa Lomaśa, both brāhmaṇas stood up from the seat,
and honored him with water for the feet, respectful offerings, water for sipping, and other things. / Lomaśa, devoted to Nārāyaṇa, was well pleased with both of them;
the best of brāhmaṇas sat upon a seat, praising Hari. / To that great-souled Lomaśa who sat on the seat with folded hands,
The two childless sages, pure [in heart], spoke with devotion to Lomaśa: / “O venerable one, knower of all dharmas, through your two feet, which should be held [in reverence] by good men,
surely this hermitage of ours has been purified. / Whatever sins were committed by us out of delusion in the past,
all of them have been destroyed through the sight of your two feet. / You are Nārāyaṇa manifest, worthy of worship even by the immortals.
Are we two mortals capable of properly performing your worship? / Whatever worship of the guest was performed by us according to our own capacity,
be well pleased with it, and forgive our fault.” / Having spoken thus, those two high-souled householder companions, best of twice-born men, / fell at the two feet of that guest.
Vyāsa said: / Then Lomaśa, best among the learned, well pleased with their devotion, [said]: / “You two are foremost among the humble, best of the twice-born, devoted to dharma.
I am exceedingly gratified by your words of humility. / A guest is said by the wise to be Brahmā, Śiva, and Viṣṇu manifest.
Such devotion to him is yours; let there be auspiciousness. / I, the guest, have been well worshipped with abundant meals.”
Vyāsa said: / Then, rising, those two brāhmaṇas at his two lotus feet / again bowed down to that sage Lomaśa and spoke.
The two brāhmaṇas said: / “O brāhmaṇa, you ought to tell the glorification of guest-worship, / performing which, liberation, though difficult to attain, is reached by human beings.”
Who is called a guest in this world, and what is the worship of him like? / What realm do both of these—the host and the guest—attain?
Lomaśa said: / Because of the honoring of forest-dwellers, students, and mendicants, / the householder's life is declared superior among all four stages of life.
Among the four stages of life, householders are considered foremost; / and they must perform the worship of guests with devotion.
The worship of guests is proclaimed the supreme duty of householders; / therefore, those householders are considered not fallen from the conduct of their stage of life.
If householders possess expertise in the worship of guests, / then what need have they for other meritorious acts?
He whose name is not known, nor lineage, nor dwelling-place, / and who arrives suddenly at the house, is called a guest by the wise.
Whether Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras, / those who arrive at the house are honored like Viṣṇu by those who perceive reality.
Those who are born of inferior classes, beginning with Cāṇḍālas, / are to be honored like Viṣṇu with water for washing feet, guest-offerings, and abundant food.
When guests arrive, if the householder is setting out on a journey, / the twice-born should nonetheless quickly offer water for feet, guest-offerings, and other [hospitalities].
He should ask after their welfare with words of gentle syllables, / or the householder should joyfully provide a meal [served] with divine jewels.
The wise man should provide a bed in a comfortable dwelling for him; / seeing him wishing to depart in the morning, he should escort him on his way.
If by the ripening of karma a householder becomes wealthy, / a guest should be honored with hospitality; that I tell you, O best of men.
When guests arrive, he should offer grass [for sitting] and other items with devotion; / in the absence of grass, he should indeed say with devotion: "Sit on the ground."
He should offer excellent water for washing the feet; / then, with sweet speech, he should ask after their welfare and health.
Then he should offer fruit and other foods with devotion for the purpose of a meal; / in its absence, the wise Brāhmaṇa should joyfully reveal [the truth],
and say: "O guest, I am a great sinner and foremost among the destitute; / I wish to show you devotion, but fate is an obstacle."
By this rule, a humble man does not abandon the worship of guests; / not fallen from his own proper conduct, he attains the declared fruit.
From whose house a guest departs unhonored, / the merit accumulated by that householder in ten million births goes to destruction.
If even a single guest is honored with a devotional disposition, / Hari instantly removes that person's sin born of ten million births.
I speak truth, I speak what is beneficial, I speak firmly with effort: / without service to guests, there is no good realm for a householder.
Truth, truth, again truth! Without worship of a visitor, / there is no good realm—none at all, none at all—for those whose duty is that of a householder.
In the Dvāpara age, there was [a man] known as Jñātidharma, beloved, / who knew all duties, and his [wife] was named Śrīvallabhā.
By him, serving his kinsmen, all duties were performed; / he made his abode in Saurāṣṭra along with his wife.
There, due to the movement of an evil planet, Indra for twelve years / did not rain water; because of that, O twice-born ones, a very great famine arose.
During that great famine, the people living in that country / all became afflicted with sorrow, and they even abandoned moral boundaries.
In that age named Dvāpara, the great yogin Jñānabhadra, / his wealth stripped away by the famine, became extremely distressed.
Seeing his sons and wife agitated by hunger, O approved among the twice-born, / he went to the slope of a mountain to gather fruits and roots for food.
At the edge of the mountain's slope, that hungry long-lived man, / O best among Brāhmaṇas, found a single gourd fruit.
Taking that fruit, that delighted leader of the twice-born, / the renowned Jñānabhadra, went swiftly to his own home.
Meanwhile, O twice-born one, when the sky was covered with clouds, / like dark blue lotuses, a rain of great downpours occurred.
His entire body drenched by that rain, a certain forest-dwelling sage, / distressed by cold, came from the forest to his house.
Seeing the guest distressed by cold, he then bowed with his head; / he gave him a seat of grass with devotion, and then water for feet and the like.
Then, with sweet speech, he remained with that guest / with a calm mind, carrying on a conversation of wisdom.
Together with his wife, who was very skilled in serving her husband, / the cowherd [Jñānabhadra] then cooked the fresh gourd with great care.
Receiving it, that virtuous woman was delighted, and having divided it into portions, she served it; / then that cowherd, weak from fasting for twenty days,
the hospitable host, joyfully gave a large portion to the guest; / then his virtuous wife, devoted to service of her husband,
joyfully gave her own portion that had fallen to her to that guest; / then, between those two magnanimous spouses, for the guest
there were two portions, and having eaten, he was well pleased, O best of the twice-born; / honored by the two like Viṣṇu with firm devotion,
taking rest right there at night, he bathed in the morning and departed; / in this way, twenty-one days passed in fasting.
Then those two magnanimous spouses underwent death; / through the power of that merit, those noble spouses
attained union with Viṣṇu, difficult to reach even for yogins; / through the power of the merit of those two, performed through worship of the guest,
the famine in that kingdom was then destroyed; / the people became exceedingly happy, free from grief and disease,
endowed with wealth, grain, and other goods, and intent on righteousness; / thieves were destroyed there, and the king was a protector of the people.
People were devoted to their own proper conduct, and clouds rained according to desire; / ten million ancestors of those two, and likewise their descendants,
attained liberation through that very deed, freed from sin; / faultless, endowed with wealth, uniquely honored by all the world,
and free from grief and disease, their lineage flourished. / Lomaśa said: The glorification of the worship of visitors has been related by me with legendary history.
What else do you wish to hear, O pleased twice-born ones? / Vyāsa said: Indeed, while that Lomaśa, rich in austerity, was speaking thus,
a black mouse seized by time came out there from its hole; / agitated with anger toward that black mouse that had emerged from the hole,
Pavitra stood up there, saying thus again and again: / "This sinful, wicked mouse at night digs at the hermitage
with masses of sharp teeth, and gnaws the property of the house; / compassion is proclaimed supreme for all social classes,
and it should be shown toward everyone, but not toward wicked creatures." / Having spoken thus, that best of the twice-born, having an offense committed [against him],
struck that mouse whose time had come with a very sharp iron arrow; / that mouse, its limbs drenched by flowing streams of blood,
fell upon the ground, O sage among the twice-born, its consciousness struck down by agony; / when that mouse fell down, that compassionate best of the twice-born,
having then raised a cry of grief, arose in haste; / bringing an excellent tulasī leaf from his own ear,
He placed [it] on the face, the head, and both ears of that mouse: / "O Mother, goddess Tulasī, who delight Govinda!"
“Bring about the highest state of this mouse that has committed sin.” / Having spoken thus, that best of the twice-born, who benefited all the world,
loudly uttered the cry: “O Hari! O Nārāyaṇa! O Ananta!” / From contact with the leaf of the tulasī plant, the mouse was freed from defilement,
and from hearing the name of Hari, it was released from the bonds of worldly existence. / Then the messengers of Mahāviṣṇu, endowed with all auspicious marks,
came swiftly with fine chariots to take him whose defilement was gone. / Ascending the divine chariot, surrounded by the hosts of Viṣṇu's messengers,
the mouse went to the supreme abode, O best of the twice-born. / Remaining for ten million thousand ages in the hermitage of Nārāyaṇa,
and attaining knowledge right there, that mouse reached liberation. / Vyāsa said: The glorification of goddess Tulasī has been told to you, O best of the twice-born.
Now tell me, O fortunate one, what do you wish to hear?

7.26.m: Jaimini said: / When the Kali yuga has arrived, exceedingly dreadful, O fortunate one, / what kind will all people be? Tell me that.
Vyāsa said: / They say the first is the Kṛta age; in it, people beginning with brāhmaṇas / were devoted to the worship of Nārāyaṇa, free from sorrow and disease,
all speaking truthful words, compassionate, long-lived, / endowed with wealth, grain, and the like, and free from violence and hypocrisy,
beneficent to others, and likewise knowers of all the scriptures. / Of such a kind were all people in the Kṛta age, O best of the twice-born.
Kings followed royal duty and protected the subjects. / Ah, who is capable of recounting the virtue and glory of the Kṛta age,
wherein no people at all uttered unrighteousness? / When the Tretā age arrived, dharma lost one quarter.
People were accompanied by a little sorrow; some had recourse to sin. / People were engaged in meditating on Viṣṇu, devoted to sacrifice and giving,
intent upon the conduct of their castes and stages of life, happy, and of sound mind. / Śūdras were tillers of the land and soil, all serving brāhmaṇas.
And the high-souled brāhmaṇas had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, / abstained from accepting gifts, were true to their promises, and had conquered their senses,
constantly engaged in austerity and vows, generous, and serving Viṣṇu. / At the conclusion of the Tretā age, when the Dvāpara age had arrived,
dharma was deprived of two quarters; men were attended by pleasure and pain. / Some were devoted to sin, and some were righteous;
some were devoid of virtues, and some possessed great virtues; / some were exceedingly wretched, and likewise some were happy.
And a brāhmaṇa would sometimes develop a longing for accepting gifts; / subjects were sometimes oppressed by kings through greed for wealth.
Twice-born men were devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu, and śūdras served the twice-born. / When dharma lost a quarter age by age, O twice-born one,
then Vyāsa, possessing the form of Viṣṇu, divided the Veda. / And in the Kali age, O foremost of vipras, the single temple of all sins,
dharma has only one quarter; all people are devoted to sin. / Brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, and śūdras are intent on wickedness;
they will be exceedingly lustful and cruel in the Kali yuga, / censuring the Vedas, and indulging in gambling and theft.
They will be immersed in intercourse with widows in the Kali yuga. / Some brāhmaṇas, for the sake of a livelihood, will practice great deceitful piety;
all will be ruled by women, indulging in intoxicating substances, / always fixated on female genitalia, and stealing the property of others,
ever covetous of food belonging to others, averse to austerity and vows; / and they will be bound to the association of heretics in the Kali yuga.
Brāhmaṇas will wear red garments, adopting the behavior of śūdras. / In Kali, high-born people who have lost their livelihood will sink to extreme baseness,
and the base, endowed with wealth, will attain high status. / All people will give gifts only to those who have rendered them favors.
Even with effort, śūdras will not provide a livelihood for brāhmaṇas. / Out of affection for a friend, people will bear false witness in Kali.
Their speech expresses unrighteous thoughts; they lament with righteous intentions; / they are backbiters, cruel, yet sweet-spoken to one's face.
Unchaste women will speak words of virtuous wives to their husbands. / Twice-born men will harm other men's wives, and sell their lineage,
and they will be sellers of daughters in the Kali yuga. / All men will be dominated by women, and women will be exceedingly fickle.
Such will they be in the Kali yuga; in Kali mortals are ill-intentioned. / The earth will yield little harvest, and the clouds will carry little water,
and they will rain out of season in the Kali yuga. / In Kali, cows will eat excrement and yield little milk, O Jaimini;
and that milk will be devoid of ghee; of this there is no doubt. / People will be intent on self-praise and devoted to censuring others;
they will have stunted limbs, and children will consume large amounts of food. / Brāhmaṇas in Kali will perform sacrifices to the ancestors for the sake of ostentation.
All will be friends in words only, as long as their purpose is not accomplished; / and seeing men devoted to dharma, they will surely all mock them.
People prosper through unrighteousness; therefore, men are devoted to sin. / Yet within ten or twelve years it perishes along with its root,
just like the swellings of water that occur during the rains. / Then people in Kali will have their youth faded;
in her fifth or sixth year, a female will bear a fetus; / and men with many children will be exceedingly sorrowful.
All will desire to take, and none at all will desire to give. / In Kali kings will be barbarians, intent on evil.
People will become of one caste for the sake of sensual objects in Kali. / In the first twilight of Kali, men censure Hari.
In the middle of the Kali age, they do not even look upon the names of Hari; / and in the Kali yuga, brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, and śūdras,
indeed all four castes, will become of a single caste. / Whenever, O best of the twice-born, there is a decline of the virtuous
and an increase of sinful mortals, then an increase [of power] in the Kali age is to be understood. / Even though this terrible Kali age has been described by me, O best of the twice-born,
nonetheless it possesses one great virtue, O best of the virtuous: / In the Kṛta age, the accomplishment of religious merit occurs in twelve years;
and in half of that in the Tretā age; in the Dvāpara age, it occurs in a month; / but in the Kali yuga, O vipra, that very [accomplishment] occurs in a single day and night.
Therefore, in the Kali yuga, the highest state belongs to man as a mortal. / Whatever fruit [is obtained] by worshipping Hari for twelve years in another age,
that fruit a mortal obtains in the Kali age merely by uttering [the name of] Hari. / The person who utters even a single name of Hari here in the Kali age—
the Kali age does not oppress him; truly, truly, there is no doubt. / Jaimini said: / Because of the absence of mental purity, every action is rendered fruitless;
"This was previously spoken by you, causing astonishment to my mind: / 'In the Kali age, all will be devoid of purity of mind.'
Explain, O guru, how their actions can all become [efficacious]. / Vyāsa said: / Whatever action a mortal performs, [whatever] duty in the Kali yuga,
he should offer that to Mahāviṣṇu, endowed with a devotional disposition. / An action offered to Viṣṇu becomes entirely imperishable.
Vyāsa said: / Thus has the entire history been related to you, O best of brāhmaṇas, / hearing which with a devotional disposition, a person attains liberation.
Sūta said: / Thus instructed by that supreme soul, Jaimini, / having become devoted to practical yoga, reached the supreme state.
This Kriyāyogasāra spoken by the great-souled Vyāsa— / the people who read it with devotion and the seekers of liberation who listen to it,
all of them, freed even from dreadful sins accumulated over many births, / attain supreme liberation; there is no doubt about this.
Whatever desires they read it [for], or the seekers of liberation listen [for], / that very [desire] they quickly obtain by the grace of the husband of Kamalā.
Having read or heard half a verse, or a single verse, / or even a quarter of a verse, a person obtains the desired fruit.
Whoever, having written it or having caused it to be written, should worship this treatise, / that person obtains the fruit of worshipping Viṣṇu himself.

May this exceedingly secret, most delightful Purāṇa, issuing from the mouth of Vyāsa, / which brings joy to the Vaiṣṇavas, / be for the pleasure of Murāri, the wielder of the discus, the master of all the worlds, / whose feet have long been praised by the foremost immortals and others.
